finding: Relative yield loss = ky x relative shortfall in crop water use. Seasonal ky for maize is 1.25 (bean 1.15, potato 1.10, winter wheat 1.00, sunflower 0.95, cotton 0.85, soybean 0.85, groundnut 0.70). The relation originates in FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 33 (S-FAO33).
Maize rainfall limits: absolute minimum 400 mm, optimum 600-1200 mm, absolute maximum 1800 mm. Kept for comparison; the stress levels use Concern (E-0003).
note: EcoCrop gives limits, not yield.

finding: Maize needs between 500 and 1200 mm over the cycle; short-season varieties withstand a minimum of 300 mm. Optimal air temperature 18-32 C.
note: Gives requirements; the only quantified yield loss is for delayed planting.

finding: Suitability classes can be related to relative yield, e.g. s1 = 1.0-0.8, s2 = 0.8-0.7, s3 = 0.7-0.6 of the best yield, 'but not necessarily these values'. Stated as examples only.
note: Supports reading suitability as relative yield only loosely.

finding: General rule for drought. Stress levels are season rainfall below 100 %, 80 % and 60 % of the crop's requirement; for maize 500, 400 and 300 mm, which are Concern's requirement and withstand-minimum (E-0003) and match the Atlas generic thresholds. The same fractions are applied to other crops. Central loss = 1.25 x rainfall shortfall (E-0001) at the middle of each band: moderate 12 %, severe 38 %, extreme 62 % (taken at half the requirement). Lower bound: top of the band under the same rule. Upper bound: middle of the band if yield fell in a straight line from the requirement to zero at 60 % of it. Derived for maize; applied to all crops until deep dives are done.
note: Assumes shortfall in crop water use is proportional to shortfall in season rainfall. Ignores timing within the season.

finding: Each degree day spent above 30 C reduced the final yield by 1 % under optimal rain-fed conditions and by 1.7 % under drought (more than 20,000 trials, 1999-2007). Model: log(yield) with station and year fixed effects; coefficients -0.01 and -0.017 per degree day above 30 C. Degree days are hourly temperatures interpolated between daily Tmin and Tmax with a sine curve, summed from sowing to 150 days after sowing.
unit: change in log yield per degree day above 30 C
locator: p. 42 abstract; p. 43 eq. 1 and text; p. 45 Methods eq. 2; SI Fig. S1 (degree days 0 to about 120)
note: Full text read 24 Nov 2026. Trials were well fertilised; the authors note nitrogen stress mutes heat response, so low-input farms may lose less. Sensitivity is highest around silking (SI Fig. S3).

finding: General rule for heat (v2.1, decision 0001, amended 24 Nov 2026). Loss = 1 - exp(-0.01 x degree days above the crop's moderate threshold, summed over its heat window), Lobell's log-yield form (E-0006); upper value with -0.017. Degree days per level from E-0123: central at the median, lower at the 25th percentile, upper at the 75th. Result: moderate 8 % (5-20), severe 34 % (19-65), extreme 64 % (50-95). Cross-check: 52-75 % kernel loss after heat at silking (E-0124). Derived for maize; applied to all crops until deep dives are done.
note: v2 (23 Nov) used 1 % x degree days, capped at 75 %; the log form follows the source and needs no cap. Interim: degree days are from Kenya only, with an assumed daily range.

finding: Conservation agriculture raised yield by 3.7 % across six major crop species against conventional tillage (933 observations, 16 countries).
note: First pass: read from the abstract only. Conservation agriculture is wider than reduced tillage with residue.

finding: Maize: 4.0 % against conventional tillage; 8.4 % where the conservation agriculture principles were combined.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: 'The largest yield benefits from CA occur in combination with low rainfall and herbicides.' Direction only; no size.
note: First pass from the abstract. Superseded by the full-text rows E-0306 to E-0310 (site-rainfall strata, p. 449, Fig. 7); keep for traceability, do not use alongside them.

finding: Performance of conservation agriculture relative to conventional practice 'improves with increasing drought severity or exposure to high temperatures'. In very wet seasons and on clay-rich soils it yields less. Direction only in the abstract.
note: First pass from the abstract. Superseded by the full-text rows E-0301 (moisture stress, p. 197, Fig. 2) and E-0303 (wet seasons, clay); keep for traceability, do not use alongside them.

finding: As E-0104 for high temperatures. Moisture and heat stress effects are non-additive and depend on soil clay content.
note: First pass from the abstract. Superseded by the full-text rows E-0302, E-0304 and E-0305 (heat stress, pp. 197-198, Figs 2-4); keep for traceability, do not use alongside them.

finding: Mulching gave the largest cereal grain-yield gain at the driest sites: mean difference 0.72 t/ha at <601 mm vs 0.21 t/ha (0.06-0.35) at 601-800 mm and 0.49 t/ha (-0.16 to 1.14, not significant) at >800 mm; 'Mulching performed better when the rainfall is less than 600 mm'. 23.4 % of mulching pairs showed no gain.
unit: t/ha grain yield difference, mulch minus control, sites <601 mm (95 % CI)
locator: p. 18 Table 3 and section 3.2.2; p. 16 Table 1 (risk); p. 20 (rainfall caveat)
note: Re-read in full text by A2 (25 Nov 2026; repository copy). Re-keyed from C2.1 to C2.2: residue mulch, mostly without a tillage contrast, is the residue part of C2.2 (C2.1 excludes residue alone). Rainfall classes are long-term site means, not stressed seasons (authors, p. 20): a dry-climate contrast, not m. Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Senegal. Stream C has the abstract finding as applicability (E-0758).

finding: Parkland trees gave the smallest mean cereal yield gain of the practices: 0.02 t/ha across all sites, and 65.6 % of pairs showed no gain (the highest risk of any practice).
unit: t/ha grain yield difference, under canopy minus open field
note: Re-read in full text by A2 (25 Nov 2026). The rainfall split is in E-0108; coppicing trees and green manure splits are E-1052 and E-1053.

finding: Parkland trees raised cereal yield at drier sites but not wetter ones: mean difference 0.36 t/ha (0.06-0.65) at <601 mm and 0.31 t/ha (0.07-0.54) at 601-800 mm, vs -0.05 t/ha (-0.35 to 0.25) at >800 mm.
unit: t/ha grain yield difference, under canopy minus open, sites <601 mm (95 % CI)
note: Re-read in full text by A2 (25 Nov 2026). Long-term site rainfall classes, not drought seasons. Discussion (p. 21) reports larger gains under Faidherbia albida than under other parkland species.

finding: Agroforestry 'significantly increased crop yield' against plots without trees (yield subset: 397 observations from 61 publications in 17 countries). Size not in the abstract.
note: Covers agroforestry as a whole, not parklands alone. Full text read by A2: yield RR 1.9 semi-arid vs 2.0 humid, no zone effect (Table 1, p. 7; also stream C E-0842). Water regulation by zone: E-1055.

finding: As E-0109; applies to tree-crop intercropping as part of agroforestry as a whole.
note: Full text read by A2: see E-0109. Water regulation by zone: E-1055.

finding: Coppicing woody legumes raised maize yield by 1.6 t/ha over unfertilised maize (non-coppicing 1.3 t/ha). Doubling or tripling of yield occurred only on low and medium potential sites. 94 publications.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only. Absolute gain, not a percentage.

finding: Herbaceous green manure legumes raised maize yield by 0.8 t/ha over unfertilised maize. 94 publications.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only. Absolute gain, not a percentage.

finding: Biochar gave 'a 25% average increase in yield in the tropics' and no effect in temperate regions; 13 % across all studies. About 1,100 comparisons from about 110 studies. Gains highest on low-pH soils.
note: Tropics defined as within 35 degrees of the equator; not Africa-specific.

finding: Alternate wetting and drying lowered rice yield by 5.4 % overall against continuous flooding. Mild AWD: yields 'not significantly reduced in most circumstances'. Severe AWD: -22.6 %. 56 studies, 528 comparisons.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: 'Cocoa yields in agroforestry systems were 25% lower than in monocultures, but total system yields were about ten times higher.' 52 articles.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: Cocoa agroforestry vs monoculture microclimate: mean daily maximum temperature 32.4 vs 34.7 C (8 studies, p < 0.05), minimum 18.6 vs 17.9 C (p < 0.001), mean 24.7 vs 25.0 C (p < 0.05); relative humidity and VPD did not differ significantly. Authors: agroforests buffer temperature extremes. No yield effect under heat is given.
unit: degrees C difference in mean daily Tmax, agroforestry minus monoculture (computed from the Table 1 means)
locator: p. 5 Table 1 (microclimate rows); p. 7 section 3.5; p. 8 Fig. 5
note: Re-read in full text by A2 (25 Nov 2026). Mechanism, not yield under heat. Soil water was lower under agroforestry (E-1056).

finding: Milk yield rose by 39 % with improved legume feeding against basal diets (72 observations). 72 studies, 780 treatment-control pairs, 15 countries. No rainfall or temperature moderator analysed.
locator: abstract and first half of text
note: Not a full meta-analysis: variances often unreported. On-station yields are not reached by most farmers. A2 full-text check: no result is split by season or dry period; the authors state that 'relative dry-season feed productivity still remains understudied' (pp. 8-9).

finding: 'Animal production per hectare' was 'significantly greater under strategic-rest grazing' than continuous grazing; weight gain per animal showed no difference. No sizes in the abstract.
note: First pass from the abstract. A2 check (25 Nov 2026): closed access, no repository full text; the abstract reports no rainfall or aridity moderator. Site data are on Dryad (10.5061/dryad.kf160cj, CC0) and could be checked for rainfall.

finding: Holistic planned grazing against season-long continuous grazing: 'no difference in plant basal cover, plant biomass and animal gain responses'.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: 'Studies with positive effect sizes tended to have higher precipitation', suggesting only some rangelands can support the practice. Direction only.
note: Abstract only: the CC BY main text could not be opened by the A2 search (publisher bot check). The supplement's dry- vs wet-year data for two primary studies are in E-1054.

finding: Silicate rock powders gave a 33 % yield gain against matched controls in Brazil (54 studies). About 80 % of observations are greenhouse, pot or incubation trials.
note: Brazil only; mostly pot trials. A2 full-text read (25 Nov 2026): field-only yield gain 20.7 % (p. 8, section 3.1, Fig. 2); no water-stress, rainfall or climate moderator was tested (p. 5, section 2.3). Some authors work for a rock-powder company (competing-interest statement).

finding: Yields increase with temperature up to 29 C for corn, 30 C for soybeans and 32 C for cotton, and temperatures above these thresholds are very harmful; the slope above the optimum is much steeper than below it. Degree days use the whole distribution of temperature within each day.
note: United States county yields. Supports a steep loss above a per-crop threshold, so a degree-day base per crop; the threshold values themselves are US-specific.

finding: Degree days above 30 C in the maize heat window, single-sine method with an assumed 12 C daily range, Kenya cube (CHIRTS-ERA5), two sowing dates, with and without a 3 C warm-offset correction. Across the four runs: moderate p25 5.1 / median 8.6 / p75 13.3; severe 21.4 / 42.1 / 62.3; extreme 70.1 / 100.9 / 180 (smallest p25, median of the medians, largest p75). Counted from the daily maximum alone the values are 4-5 times higher.
unit: degree days above the moderate threshold
note: Interim. Kenya only, all land cells (no crop mask), fixed sowing dates, assumed daily range, day rules not agreed. To be replaced by pipeline output once it reads daily minimum temperature. Script: OneDrive Technical Development/Adaptation & Production Benefits/Stress tiers and heat loss/scripts/heat_dd_by_tier.py.

finding: Daytime heating to about 33-40 C at ear level for 15 days cut harvestable kernels by a mean of 51.8 % just before silking and 74.5 % during silking, across temperate, tropical and crossed hybrids in two field experiments.
note: Argentina field experiments. Kernel number, not yield; one ear per plant. Cross-check for the extreme heat loss (64 % central under the log-yield rule).

finding: Meta-regression of the CA-to-conventional maize yield ratio (1042 observations, 85 sites, 1984-2013; 84.7 % south-east Africa). Moisture stress is the growing-season precipitation balance (rainfall minus Penman-Monteith PET) of each observed season. CA yields are generally higher where the balance is below 200 mm, and the advantage grows as the season gets drier.
unit: mm precipitation balance below which CA generally outyields conventional
note: Response ratio only, from a continuous surface: not m. The supplement holds the meta-dataset (B.1) and the bootstrapped coefficients (Table A.6), from which arm-level stress contrasts could be re-derived in phase 2. Stress is measured per season, not by site climate.

finding: Heat stress is growing degree days above 30 C around anthesis, as ln(GDD30+ + 1). Under drought, CA increasingly outperforms conventional practice as heat stress rises. With a rainfall surplus, rising heat reduces CA's relative performance, which turns negative on clay-rich soils. Heat and moisture effects are non-additive and depend on clay content.
note: Direction and shape only; values are read from a figure surface (soil clay set at 25 % in Figs 3-4).

finding: In very wet seasons and on clay-rich soils (clay above 50 %), CA yields less than conventional practice; the authors attribute this to waterlogging.
note: Excess-rainfall finding: hazard left blank (the tables cover drought and heat only). Relevant to the sign of m in wet seasons.

finding: Under high heat stress, the relative yield benefit of CA narrows as more nitrogen is applied to both systems, but stays positive even at very high N rates. With little heat stress (under 1 GDD30+), more N improves CA's relative performance.
note: Shown for a 154 mm rainfall surplus and 25 % clay. A moderator to carry into strata, not a separate value.

finding: Full CA, with crop diversification, changed less under heat stress than no-till or reduced tillage with cover alone. Without diversification, rising heat and falling precipitation balance increasingly improved CA's relative performance.
note: Diversification is a stability moderator: decide in phase 2 whether to stratify C2.2 by it.

finding: CA vs conventional tillage yield across crops at sites with average seasonal rainfall below 400 mm (24 observations, 5 studies).
note: The strata are classes of the site's average seasonal rainfall, not stressed seasons, so this is a dry-climate contrast, not m. The open dataset (CIRAD 10.18167/DVN1/DLTQWR) records actual seasonal rainfall for each row, so a season-level re-analysis is possible in phase 2.

finding: As E-0306, at sites with 400-800 mm average seasonal rainfall (431 observations, 48 studies).
note: Site climate class; see E-0306.

finding: As E-0306, at sites with 800-1,200 mm average seasonal rainfall (375 observations, 45 studies).
note: Reference class for the drier strata. The effect here is significantly lower than below 400 mm (P < 0.05).

finding: As E-0306, at sites with more than 1,200 mm average seasonal rainfall (103 observations, 9 studies): yields lower under CA.
note: Wet-climate finding; hazard blank. Consistent with E-0303.

finding: Rainfall interacts with soil texture. Below 800 mm seasonal rainfall, CA outyielded CT on all soil types. At 800-1,200 mm it did so only on coarse soils (4.7 %, CI 2.8-6.7). Above 1,200 mm the effect was negative on medium and fine soils and zero on sandy soils.
unit: percent yield change (CA vs CT), coarse soils, 800-1,200 mm
note: Soil texture is a moderator for C2.2 strata (with Steward 2018 clay content, E-0302).

finding: Langgewens dryland wheat LTE, 1976-2020 (395 mm mean annual rainfall, about 80 % in April-September). Over 1996-2020, seasonal rainfall explained 37 % of wheat yield variation under mouldboard ploughing and 21 % under the infrequent shallow-tine then no-till sequence. Yields fell with seasonal rainfall until 2013 but not afterwards.
unit: percent of yield variance explained by seasonal rainfall (R2)
note: Lower R2 under reduced tillage is a hint of buffering, not a stress contrast. Yearly yields are plotted as 4-year rolling means (Fig. 3); single years only for 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2020 (Fig. 4). Preprint, not peer reviewed. Season-level arm yields need the WCDoA data (request pending Pete's go).

finding: Authors found no straightforward relationship between yields and seasonal precipitation: cumulative growing-season rainfall explained 2-37% of between-season yield variation in maize and soybean, with non-significant regression slopes.
unit: % of between-season yield variation explained by seasonal rainfall (maize and soybean, all arms)
note: Table A.4 (supplement, PDF p. 13) cumulative rainfall maize seasons, Siaya&Nyabeda / Kibugu (mm): SR2006 1194/947; LR2007 713/593; LR2008 889/534; LR2009 562/469; LR2010 891/721; LR2011 800/581; LR2012 1098/797; LR2014 1021/503; LR2015 1039/710; LR2016 957/528. Soybean seasons: SR2007 543/539; SR2008 539/383; SR2009 652/435; SR2010 475/411; SR2011 802/743; SR2013 616/487; SR2014 466/382; SR2015 785/652. Because rainfall did not predict yield, low-rainfall seasons cannot be assumed to be stress seasons without further checks. Site: Kibugu (Embu County), Nyabeda and Siaya (Siaya County), Kenya. Stress as defined by authors: None. Seasonal rainfall reported as cumulative CHIRPS rainfall from 14 d before planting to harvest plus a rainfall-irregularity index (Table A.4); no season is labelled stressed or normal.. Stress seasons: not identified by authors. Normal seasons: not identified by authors. Yearly arm yields: p. 22, Fig. 2 (graph only: per site, 4 arms UC, UC+BC, FC, FC+BC, every season); p. 23, Table 2 (biochar increment per season pooled across sites and fertiliser). Seasons: 10 maize, 8 soybean (SR2006-LR2016); 3 replicate blocks per site, 3 sites.

finding: Biochar (50+50 Mg/ha applied SR2006 and LR2007) raised maize yield by 1.17 Mg/ha averaged over seasons; per-season increments 0.55-2.93 Mg/ha, significant in 8 of 10 seasons.

note: Per-season increments (Mg/ha, SE): SR2006 0.55 (0.29); LR2007 0.77 (0.30); LR2008 2.93 (0.54); LR2009 1.68 (0.32); LR2010 0.82; LR2011 0.89; LR2012 0.83; LR2014 1.00; LR2015 0.79; LR2016 1.44. Increments are absolute and pooled across sites, so arm-level proportional losses need Fig. 2 (graph) or site data. stress_level left blank because the row pools sites with different rainfall. Site: Kibugu (Embu County), Nyabeda and Siaya (Siaya County), Kenya. Stress as defined by authors: None. Seasonal rainfall reported as cumulative CHIRPS rainfall from 14 d before planting to harvest plus a rainfall-irregularity index (Table A.4); no season is labelled stressed or normal.. finding: Between-season coefficient of variation of maize yield was lower with biochar (UC 57.3% vs UC+BC 21.5%; FC 37.2% vs FC+BC 25.5%); authors conclude productivity was 'more reliable under fluctuating weather conditions'.
unit: % CV of between-season random effect, maize UC+BC (comparator UC 57.3%)
note: Table 3 maize SD of season random effect (Mg/ha): UC 0.75, UC+BC 0.63, FC 0.89, FC+BC 1.05 (SD higher with biochar under fertiliser; CV lower because mean is higher). Mixed-model estimate across sites. Not a stress-season contrast; a variability metric. Site: Kibugu (Embu County), Nyabeda and Siaya (Siaya County), Kenya. Stress as defined by authors: None. finding: Soybean between-season CV was lower with biochar (UC 46.0% vs UC+BC 34.5%; FC 47.3% vs FC+BC 32.5%); authors say biochar effects on yield reliability were greater for soybean than maize. Mean biochar increment 0.43 Mg/ha (0.14-0.78 per season).
unit: % CV of between-season random effect, soybean UC+BC (comparator UC 46.0%)
note: Table 3 soybean SD (Mg/ha): UC 0.14, UC+BC 0.47, FC 0.52, FC+BC 0.78. Soybean per-season increments (Table 2): SR2007 0.78; SR2008 0.37; SR2009 0.42; SR2010 0.26; SR2011 0.14; SR2013 0.32; SR2014 0.56; SR2015 0.56 (significant 5 of 8). Soybean-season rainfall in Table A.4 (see first Katterer 2019 row). Site: Kibugu (Embu County), Nyabeda and Siaya (Siaya County), Kenya. Stress as defined by authors: None. Seasonal rainfall reported as cumulative CHIRPS rainfall from 14 d before planting to harvest plus a rainfall-irregularity index (Table A.4); no season is labelled stressed or normal.. Stress seasons: not identified by authors. Normal seasons: not identified by authors. Yearly arm yields: p. 22, Fig. 2 (graph only: per site, 4 arms UC, UC+BC, FC, FC+BC, every season); p. 23, Table 2 (biochar increment per season pooled across sites and fertiliser). Seasons: 8 soybean seasons; 3 reps x 3 sites.

finding: Crops in biochar plots were visibly less affected by dry periods (less leaf curling and senescence) but this was not measured; biochar raised water-holding capacity by about 5 mm in the top 20 cm, and authors state yields were greater 'even under adverse rainfall conditions'.
unit: mm extra soil water storage in top 20 cm with biochar
note: Qualitative observation only; the adverse-rainfall seasons are not named. WHC difference 0.025 g water per g soil. Site: Kibugu (Embu County), Nyabeda and Siaya (Siaya County), Kenya. Stress as defined by authors: None. Seasonal rainfall reported as cumulative CHIRPS rainfall from 14 d before planting to harvest plus a rainfall-irregularity index (Table A.4); no season is labelled stressed or normal.. Yearly arm yields: p. 22, Fig. 2 (graph only: per site, 4 arms UC, UC+BC, FC, FC+BC, every season); p. 23, Table 2 (biochar increment per season pooled across sites and fertiliser). Seasons: 10 maize, 8 soybean.

finding: SR-2016 had a very late start of rains and low precipitation in Embu and Siaya, so the fields were left fallow 'to avoid non-representative treatment effects'; no yields were collected in the one season the authors describe as dry.
note: No seasonal rainfall amounts reported; only mean annual rainfall (Embu 1200 mm, Siaya about 1350 mm, Kwale about 1050 mm). The stress season was deliberately not cropped, so this paper gives no stress-season arm yields. Site: Embu, Kwale and Siaya counties, Kenya (6-8 smallholder farms). Stress as defined by authors: Qualitative only: very late onset of rains and low precipitation in SR-2016; no threshold.. Stress seasons: SR-2016 (Embu, Siaya) - not cropped. Normal seasons: LR-2015, SR-2015, LR-2016, LR-2017 (Embu, Siaya); LR-2015, LR-2016, LR-2017 (Kwale); not labelled normal by authors. finding: Across seasons and fertiliser treatments, biochar at 1, 5 and 10 Mg/ha raised maize yield by 1.0, 2.6 and 4.0 Mg/ha; absolute responses were similar across the four seasons and uncorrelated with control yield (p 0.14-0.89).
unit: Mg/ha absolute maize yield increase (1 to 10 Mg/ha biochar vs control)
note: Control (no biochar, no fertiliser) mean 0.70 Mg/ha. Intro (p. 2) cites Katterer et al. 2019 as showing biochar gains under favorable and unfavorable rainfall. Authors say inter-season yield variation was much lower than in the 2019 trial. No stress-season contrast possible. Site: Embu, Kwale and Siaya counties, Kenya (6-8 smallholder farms). Stress as defined by authors: None for the cropped seasons.. Stress seasons: none cropped. Normal seasons: LR-2015, SR-2015, LR-2016, LR-2017 (Embu, Siaya); LR-2015, LR-2016, LR-2017 (Kwale); not labelled normal by authors. Yearly arm yields: p. 7, Fig. 2 (graph only: per site and season, 0/1/5/10 Mg/ha biochar x +/- fertiliser). Seasons: 4 seasons (3 at Kwale); 3 replicate blocks per farm.

finding: In 2020 (546 mm, three dry spells early in the cycle) fertilised rice under CA yielded more than under conventional tillage (CA+Stylo 2147.0, CA Maize+legume 2254.1 vs CT 1434.9 kg/ha; P=0.002).
unit: kg/ha rice yield, CA arms, F1 (comparator CT 1434.9)
locator: HAL ms p. 23, Table 6; p. 24, section 3.5; p. 17, Table 3
note: 2020 is the sixth year of CA (after a transition period). Authors call 2020 unfavorable in Table 3/section 3.1 and rather unfavorable in section 3.5. Section 3.5 gives all CA systems 2035-2762 vs CT 1339-1579 kg/ha (F1). CA = no-till with cover crops (stylo, pigeon pea, etc.) and residue retention; CT = ploughing with residue removal. Rice tiers not applied (maize tiers only). Also a C2.1 contrast (legume cover in CA). Site: M'be AfricaRice station, Bouake, Cote d'Ivoire. Stress as defined by authors: Table 3: seasonal ranking from rainfall P and P-ETP (one week before sowing to harvest) and dry periods (<1 mm/day average); very unfavourable = P <500 mm or a period with P-ETP < -100 mm; unfavourable/rather unfavourable/favourable classes also defined.. Stress seasons: Summer (June sowing): 2016 very unfavourable (driest; 55-day dry spell); 2020 unfavourable/rather unfavourable (546 mm, three dry spells); 2015 unfavourable (720 mm, two early dry spells). Normal seasons: Summer 2017, 2018, 2019 rather favourable to very favourable (P 666, 922, 877 mm). Yearly arm yields: HAL ms p. 23, Table 6 (CT vs CA+Stylo vs CA Maize+legume, by year and fertiliser); p. 22, Fig. 3; p. 20, Table 5 (systems pooled). Seasons: 6 summer seasons 2015-2020 (F0 only 2017-2020); 4 reps 2015-16, 3 reps from 2017 (system 5.1: 2).

finding: In 2020 without fertiliser, CA rice also out-yielded CT (CA+Stylo 1834.9, CA Maize+legume 2021.3 vs CT 1350.3 kg/ha), significant only at p<0.10 (P=0.090).
unit: kg/ha rice yield, CA arms, F0 (comparator CT 1350.3)
locator: HAL ms p. 23, Table 6; p. 24, Fig. 4
note: Abstract gives CA 1835-2021 (F0) and 2147-2254 (F1) vs CT 1350 and 1435 kg/ha. F0 plots started in 2017 on plots fertilised in 2015-16. Also a C2.1 contrast (legume cover in CA). Site: M'be AfricaRice station, Bouake, Cote d'Ivoire. Stress as defined by authors: Table 3: seasonal ranking from rainfall P and P-ETP (one week before sowing to harvest) and dry periods (<1 mm/day average); very unfavourable = P <500 mm or a period with P-ETP < -100 mm; unfavourable/rather unfavourable/favourable classes also defined.. Stress seasons: Summer (June sowing): 2016 very unfavourable (driest; 55-day dry spell); 2020 unfavourable/rather unfavourable (546 mm, three dry spells); 2015 unfavourable (720 mm, two early dry spells). Normal seasons: Summer 2017, 2018, 2019 rather favourable to very favourable (P 666, 922, 877 mm). Yearly arm yields: HAL ms p. 23, Table 6 (CT vs CA+Stylo vs CA Maize+legume, by year and fertiliser); p. 22, Fig. 3; p. 20, Table 5 (systems pooled). Seasons: 4 summer seasons for F0 (2017-2020); 3 reps.

finding: In 2016, the driest season (55-day dry spell after emergence), fertilised rice yield was low in both CA+Stylo (782.8) and CT (653.8 kg/ha), with no significant difference (P=0.497), one year after CA began.
locator: HAL ms p. 23, Table 6; p. 20, section 3.3 and Table 5; p. 17, Table 3
