finding: Makueni, Kenya: in dry OND 2014 (172 mm, erratic after onset) CA pillars had 'no detectable effect' on yields; in wetter El Nino OND 2015 (386 mm) reduced tillage raised yield 561.85 -> 1273.52 kg/ha (+126.7%). Authors summarise reduced tillage as +250 kg/ha in dry Malawi and +700 kg/ha in wet Kenya.
unit: percent yield change vs control, Kenya wet season 2015
note: Stress as defined by the source: Kenya OND 2014 = 172 mm TAMSAT with <20 mm in 10 d after onset (dry); OND 2015 = 386 mm (El Nino, wet). 103 farmers; few data on ground cover in Kenya. Opposite-sign hint: in this Kenyan site the tillage benefit showed in the wet, not the dry season.

finding: Zambia household panel (RALS 2015 + ENIAS 2016): the El Nino shock cut maize yield ~20% (coef -0.18 to -0.23). Minimum soil disturbance raised average yields (coef 0.362-0.386***) but MSD x RainDev = -2.211*** (FE) / -1.793*** (CRE): 'the average positive effect of MSD on maize yield disappears when observed rainfall deviates from the long run average'.
unit: coefficient on ln(maize yield): minimum soil disturbance x rainfall deviation (FE; CRE -1.793)
note: Stress as defined by the source: Shock = Nov 2015-Feb 2016 rainfall below the ward's long-term minimum for that period (58% of households); RainDev = absolute % deviation of season rainfall from 1983-2016 mean (ARC2). ~60% of deviations in sample were positive (wet), so the MSD interaction mixes wet and dry deviations; authors note most farmers do not combine MSD with residue retention. Published version: Environment and Development Economics 2021 (not read). No DOI on the working paper.

finding: Same model: household grows trees/shrubs (agroforestry) has no significant average yield effect (CRE -0.118*) but Trees/shrubs x RainDev = +0.944** (CRE; FE +0.332 n.s.); 'Agroforestry is the only practice that provides positive yield benefits even under rainfall conditions that deviate from the long run average'.
unit: coefficient on ln(maize yield): trees/shrubs x rainfall deviation (CRE; FE 0.332 ns)
locator: p.22 Table 5 col 4; p.23 text; appendix p.~35 robustness rows
note: Stress as defined by the source: Shock = Nov 2015-Feb 2016 rainfall below the ward's long-term minimum for that period (58% of households); RainDev = absolute % deviation of season rainfall from 1983-2016 mean (ARC2). 'Trees/shrubs grown' is a household-level indicator, not plot-level; type (Faidherbia, Gliricidia, fruit trees, fallows) not specified, so mapping to C3.1 vs C3.2 is uncertain - Pending expert review. Significant only in CRE.

finding: Zambia RILS panel 2004-2008 (8,424 plot obs., CRE): minimum soil disturbance has no significant yield effect with or without a false-onset shock (coef 0.10 without vs 0.08 with) or a hot season (0.06 vs 0.08), and no effect on the probability of very low yields.
unit: coefficient on ln(maize yield), MSD under false-onset shock (n.s.)
locator: AgEcon copy p.17-19, Table 6; p.20 (Table 7 low-yield probability)
note: Stress as defined by the source: False onset of rains (ARC2 dekadal); growing-season max temperature >= 28 C (ECMWF). MSD adoption only ~6% of plots; MSD defined without residue requirement. Heat interaction also n.s.

finding: Legume intercropping (LEGINT) raised maize yield (coef 0.134** in normal seasons) and much more in very hot seasons (0.884*** when growing-season Tmax >= 28 C); also 0.225 vs 0.244 with/without false onset. LEGINT 'decreases low yield probability even more under a temperature shock'.
unit: coefficient on ln(maize yield): legume intercrop under Tmax >= 28 C (0.134 otherwise)
locator: AgEcon copy p.18-19 Table 6 (Tmax28 interactions); p.20 text
note: Stress as defined by the source: Growing-season maximum temperature >= 28 C (ECMWF dekadal temperature). Legume intercrop is a living-cover/diversification practice; mapping to C2.1 (living soil cover) is a judgement - Pending expert review. Heat flag is seasonal Tmax, not flowering-window heat.

finding: Malawi IHPS panel (2013, 2016) + 2015 flood survey: drought cut maize yield 32-34% (value/ha 42-44%); legume intercropping is the only SLM practice with robust protection - on intercropped plots drought maize-yield losses fall to about 14% (value/ha losses 12-18%).
unit: percent maize yield loss in drought on legume-intercropped plots (32-34 % without)
locator: Results text (section on SLM x shock); Table 3 coefficients are images, not read
note: Stress as defined by the source: Flowering-period rainfall (dekads 5-8 after onset, ARC2) >30% below long-term mean; shock = absolute % deviation beyond that; >35% of 2016 plots affected. Read via HTML full text (tables as images). Mapping legume intercrop to C2.1 Pending expert review. Same paper: minimum soil disturbance (<1.5% adoption) no significant effect; bunds ~20% lower maize yield under drought.

finding: Same Malawi panel: minimum soil disturbance had no significant effect on crop production under drought or flood; adoption was <1.5% across the three years, limiting power.
note: Stress as defined by the source: Flowering-period rainfall >30% below long-term mean (ARC2). Null result with very low adoption; not evidence of absence.

finding: Southern Malawi (Machinga/Balaka), 2015/16 El Nino: hybrid maize on CA plots yielded 899.6 kg/ha (expected 2882.7; -68.8%) vs 392.2 kg/ha on non-CA plots (expected 1876.1; -79.1%); total crop failure 8.4% of CA plots vs 17.3% non-CA. Authors: CA and non-CA farmers 'experienced similar perceived decreases in yields' except cowpeas.
unit: percent yield vs farmer-expected yield on CA plots (-79.1 % non-CA)
locator: p.7 Table 5; p.6-7 text; Supplementary Table 1 (not read)
note: Stress as defined by the source: 2015/16 El Nino drought season, southern Malawi. 201-household survey (104 CA / 97 non-CA), recall yields; 'expected' yields are farmer-stated, so % decrease is relative to self-reported norm; CA farmers wealthier and more often male - selection not controlled. Cowpea: CA -46.6% vs non-CA -73.7%.

finding: US Corn Belt satellite (Landsat) yields, >150,000 field-years, causal forest: long-term conservation tillage +3.3% maize (95% CI 3.1-3.4) and +0.74% soybean; benefits were larger than average where baseline late-season (Jul-Aug) soil moisture was low; very wet early-season soils reduced benefits. Conditional effects ranged -1.3% to +8.1% (maize, 5th-95th pct).
unit: percent maize yield change (mean; 5th-95th percentile of conditional effects)
note: Stress as defined by the source: Gradient of baseline late-season soil moisture and weather covariates (no named drought year). Outside Africa; high-input commercial maize; tillage class from satellite residue mapping, residue retention implied. Dry-condition effect only shown graphically.

finding: Western US Corn Belt (NE, KS, SD, ND), satellite yields 2008-2020: long-term low-till raised rainfed maize yield 9.9% (95% CI 9.68-10.14) but had no significant effect on irrigated fields (-0.008 t/ha); largest gains with low early-season precipitation and sandy soils - 'low till helps most in more arid conditions'.
unit: percent rainfed maize yield change (95 % CI); irrigated ns
note: Stress as defined by the source: Rainfed vs irrigated contrast (water-limited vs not); early-season precipitation gradient. Outside Africa. Rainfed-vs-irrigated is a water-limitation contrast, not a drought-year contrast; 6.3% of rainfed obs. showed penalties.

finding: US Corn Belt, >90,000 fields 2019-2020, satellite yields + causal forest: 3+ years of cover cropping associated with -5.5% maize and -3.5% soybean yield; maize losses larger with lower April (spring) rainfall, soybean losses larger with lower April and August rainfall and warmer Junes - i.e. penalties grow in drier/hotter conditions.
unit: percent maize yield change, mean effect (larger losses with low April rain)
note: Stress as defined by the source: Gradient of April/August precipitation and June temperature/VPD in 2019-2020 (no named drought year). Outside Africa; winter cover crops before cash crop (water use before planting). Opposite sign to buffering: cover crops worsen dry-spring losses. Cites Garba et al. 2022: cover crops cut soil water at planting by 18% in dryland systems.

finding: Yayu, Ethiopia, 54 plots: median shrub yields fell 2014 -> 2016 across the landscape. Normal year (2014): canopy openness negative (p<0.05) and shade diversity negative (p<0.01). Shock years (2015-16): max-temperature anomaly during berry development most influential; leguminous shade broadly positive, and its interaction with canopy openness 'especially influential on yields, with strongly positive impacts at high canopy openness'; canopy openness switched from linear negative (normal) to positive non-linear (shock).
locator: p.2-3 sections 2.1-2.2, Fig. 3b-c, Fig. 4g-h; p.4 discussion
note: Stress as defined by the source: 2015/16 El Nino: ERA5 Tmax anomaly high from berry development 2015 through 2016; drier dry season (Dec-Apr) 2015; 2014 = normal. No effect sizes in kg/ha in text (coefficients in Tables S1-S3, not read). Shade is a gradient (forest coffee), not shade vs full sun. Effects of shade on shock-year yield were mixed; 'there is not an optimal canopy openness'.

finding: Same Yayu farms: coffee incomes fell to 29.5% +/- 18.0% (2015) and 19.5% +/- 10.0% (2016) of 2014 incomes; farmers with the largest income losses were at 1600-1700 m 'in larger patch areas with lower canopy openness' (i.e. denser shade).
note: Stress as defined by the source: 2015/16 El Nino (heat + drought), vs 2014 baseline. Income not yield; denser shade co-varies with forest patch and poor infrastructure - confounded. Author list beyond first six not checked.

finding: Bahia, Brazil cabruca (cocoa under thinned forest shade), 31 random farms: 2015-16 El Nino drought killed 15% (+/-2.3 SE) of cocoa trees (normally <1%) and cut potential yield 89% (242 -> 26 kg/ha). Mortality showed no relationship with shade-tree number (p=0.81) or basal area (p=0.81); yield loss not related to shade in single-variable models (shade-tree number p=0.39, basal area p=0.10).
unit: % cocoa tree mortality (no relation with shade density)
locator: Results 'Tree mortality' Table 1; 'Pod loss' Table 2; Discussion
note: Stress as defined by the source: Drought days = 30-day rain < 30-day PET; Aug 2015-Aug 2016 rain 770 mm (53% below 1621 mm mean); SPEI < -2 in 4 months (min -3.2). Outside Africa. All farms shaded (no full-sun comparator); shade-density gradient only. Yield from pod counts, not harvest.

finding: Cluster-randomised evaluation of community-based rangeland management (combined herding + planned rotational grazing), Namibia Northern Communal Areas: overall ITT effects on rangeland were negative (dry-season herbaceous biomass coef -0.78 log, p<0.001). In low-rainfall grazing areas the negative effect was smaller: treatment x low-rainfall = +0.68 (SE 0.26, p=0.014; RI p=0.124) for dry-season fresh biomass and +0.58 (p=0.007) for dry-season herbaceous canopy cover.
unit: coefficient on ln(dry-season fresh plant biomass): treatment x low-rainfall area
locator: Extended Data Table 7 Panel B; Methods 'Heterogeneous treatment effects analysis' (WP p.16); main text p.~6 (Extended Data Table 6)
note: Stress as defined by the source: Grazing area 'low rainfall' = below median of % difference between project-period (2010-14) mean rainfall and 2000-2010 mean. Published as Communications Earth & Environment 2022 (10.1038/s43247-022-00361-5, not read). Randomisation-inference p-values not significant; heterogeneity is exploratory. Herd productivity x low rainfall +0.20 n.s.; household 'resilience' index x low rain +0.28 (p=0.028). Incursions by outside herds undermined planned grazing.

finding: Msinga, KwaZulu-Natal, census of ~3,000 communal households: in the 2015-16 drought cattle herds lost 43% and goats 29%; effects of high stocking rates and poor resource condition on mortality and herd growth 'were apparent during the drought year of 2016, but not the other years'; larger herds had lower mortality.
unit: % cattle herd lost in 2015-16 drought (all farmers)
note: Stress as defined by the source: 2015-16 drought year (vs other census years). Stocking rate is one element of G1.2 ('stocking at/below capacity'); this is stocking/condition, not rotational grazing per se. Abstract read via search-result reproduction; magnitudes of the stocking effect not read.

finding: Northern Kenya communal conservancies: planned (time-controlled rotational) grazing improved cattle weight gain by >71% 'during dry periods when cattle were in relatively poor condition', alongside +17% NDVI and 45-234% higher herbaceous cover/richness.
unit: % higher cattle weight gain in dry periods (lower bound)
note: Stress as defined by the source: Seasonal dry periods (not a named drought year). Already registered as S-ODADI2017 (yield_benefit); this row only flags the dry-period livestock contrast. Dry season is seasonal, not a drought anomaly.

finding: Coppicing (pruned, mostly legume) trees in crop fields: mean grain-yield difference 0.43 t/ha at <601 mm, -0.29 t/ha (n.s.) at 601-800 mm and 0.46 t/ha at >800 mm; 44.3% of pairs showed no gain (D <= 0).
unit: t/ha grain yield difference (treatment - control), 95% CI
note: Stress as defined by the source: Long-term mean annual rainfall class of the site: low <601 mm, medium 601-800 mm, high >800 mm (p.16); not season rainfall. Non-monotonic rainfall pattern; the authors' abstract summarises this as better yields where rainfall >800 mm. 601-800 mm: -0.29 (-0.75-0.17); >800 mm: 0.46 (0.21-0.72).

finding: Green-manure legumes: no trials at sites <601 mm; mean difference -0.03 t/ha (CI -1.0 to 0.95) at 601-800 mm vs 0.79 t/ha (0.59-1.00) at >800 mm. Authors say green manure was probably not tested in drier areas because the legumes could not be grown there, and water is likely limiting below 600 mm.
unit: t/ha grain yield difference (treatment - control), 95% CI
locator: p.18 Table 3; p.18 sec 3.2.2; p.21 discussion
note: Gap marker for the driest class. Stress as defined by the source: Long-term mean annual rainfall class of the site: low <601 mm, medium 601-800 mm, high >800 mm (p.16); not season rainfall. The value is the >800 mm class; no evidence at all for the driest class. This is an evidence gap, not evidence that the practice works in drought.

finding: Supplementary data split by year type. Badgery 2016a (Australia, AI 0.68): HPG vs continuous plant cover was 82.9 vs 83.5%, 92.1 vs 85.8% and 99.1 vs 91.9% in dry years (low/med/high productivity) vs 93.5 vs 93.5, 97.3 vs 94.0 and 99.1 vs 96.3% in wet years; dry-year biomass was 1313-2275 vs 1125-1475 kg/ha. Derner 2008 (USA, AI 0.37): cattle gain 0.82 vs 0.81 kg/hd/d in the dry year, 0.83 vs 0.88 in the average year and 0.88 vs 0.91 in the wet year.
unit: percent plant cover; kg DM/ha; kg/head/day
locator: Supporting Information Table S1 (figshare 5357605, file tarf_a_1358213_sm4419.pdf)
note: Stress as defined by the source: Dry vs wet (and average) years as labelled by the primary authors. Read the supplement only (main text not reachable). The primary studies are outside Africa. HPG kept slightly more cover in dry years at one site, and cattle gain did not differ in the dry year; small n. The Africa rows in S1 (Clatworthy 1984, Gammon 1978, Zimbabwe) have no year-type split.

finding: Water regulation (infiltration plus soil moisture) improved more in semi-arid zones, RR 1.7 (1.5-2.1), than in humid zones, RR 1.2 (1.1-1.3). Soil moisture alone RR 1.6 (27 studies, 62 obs; 70% of obs > 1); infiltration RR 2.7. Crop yield and soil moisture correlated negatively but not significantly (rs = -0.294, N = 12, P = 0.354), a sign of tree-crop water competition.
locator: p.7 Table 1 (water regulation column); p.11 sec 3.4; p.13 (Spearman rs); p.7 Fig. 2
note: Mechanism evidence. Keyed to C3.2 because the pool is dominated by alley cropping, biomass transfer and planted fallows; parklands are included (C3.1). Stress as defined by the source: Agro-ecological zone: semi-arid vs humid. Mechanism evidence only; no microclimate or temperature synthesis. The soil-moisture CI is printed as '1.1-1.2', which is inconsistent with RR 1.6 (likely a typo). Authors flag publication bias for water regulation (tau = -0.234, P < 0.001).

finding: Soil volumetric water content was lower under cocoa agroforestry than in monocultures: 20.1 vs 21.8% (6 studies, p < 0.01), consistent with water use by shade trees.
unit: percentage points volumetric water content (AF minus monoculture)
note: Stress as defined by the source: none; season not stated. An opposite-sign mechanism for drought (competition for soil water). It is consistent with Abdulai et al. 2018 (S-ABDULAI2017) finding cocoa agroforestry less resilient in drought.

finding: Machine-learning synthesis of CA vs conventional tillage: CA and no-till were more likely to raise yield where the growing-season precipitation balance is negative. For winter wheat, the probability of a yield gain from CA was 56% in dry regions vs 47% in wet regions, with plausible relative change -0.11 to +0.51 (dry) vs -0.15 to +0.17 (wet). Residue retention was the strongest positive management factor. In humid regions the advantage disappears and can reverse on soils prone to waterlogging.
unit: % probability CA yield > CT (winter wheat, dry region); wet region 47%
note: Stress as defined by the source: Dry region = cumulative growing-season precipitation minus PET < 0 mm; wet region > 0 mm (climate, not single seasons). A climate-zone contrast, not drought-year vs normal-year. The paper states that tropical regions often have a 75% chance of a no-till yield loss for maize, sorghum and soybean (p.3), and that CA has a 25% chance of >30% gains in much of Africa for some crops. Crop-specific maps are in the supplement (not read).

finding: Straw mulching raised wheat yield by 20% at low seasonal water input (<250 mm) and 15% at high (>250 mm); for maize the straw-mulch effect was about 20% regardless of water input (CI +-18% at low vs +-8% at high water input).
unit: % yield increase vs no mulch (wheat, water input <250 mm)
locator: p.4 Results 'Effects of mulching ... at different water input levels', Fig. 2A-B
note: Straw mulch is the residue part of C2.2. Stress as defined by the source: Seasonal water input (rain + irrigation) split at the median: wheat 250 mm, maize 370 mm. Straw mulch alone, with no tillage contrast (residue part of C2.2). Data are mostly from China. Water input is a site/season property, not a drought-year contrast. Plastic mulch results are not relevant to the register.

finding: The straw-mulch benefit fell at higher growing-season temperature: in maize it was 60% at low temperature (12.7-19.1 C) and 18% at high temperature (19.1-30.4 C). In wheat, straw beat plastic mulch at high temperature (16.3-25.5 C) but not at low temperature.
unit: % maize yield increase vs no mulch at high season temperature (19.1-30.4 C)
locator: p.5 'Effects of mulching at different temperature', Fig. 8A-B
note: Straw mulch is the residue part of C2.2. Stress as defined by the source: Mean air temperature over the growing season, split at the median (maize 19.1 C). Mostly cool-season effects (mulch warms or cools soil). The 60% at low temperature conflicts with the 20% overall maize straw effect in the same paper; check Fig. 8 before use. This is not a heat-stress (Tmax in the sensitive window) contrast.

finding: Grazing-management changes raised infiltration by 59.3 +- 7.3% overall: extended rest +67.9 +- 8.5% (n = 140), reduced stocking +42.0 +- 10.8% (n = 63), added grazing complexity +34 +- 14% (n = 17). Humid sites (AI > 0.65; n = 25) had no negative response ratios, and regression showed 'a greater effect of grazing management in environments that are more humid' (slight, n.s.). Mean annual precipitation had no significant effect.
locator: Abstract; Results, Fig. 3b; Table 2 (aridity/MAP regression); Supplementary Fig. S3 not read
note: Mechanism evidence. Stress as defined by the source: Aridity index (humid > 0.65) and mean annual precipitation. Mechanism (water capture), not livestock output. Complexity n is 18 (12 expts) in Results vs 17 (11) in the abstract. As with Hawkins 2017, benefits lean to wetter sites. Read through WebFetch of the publisher HTML.

finding: Grazing vs ungrazed in global grasslands: grazing cut GPP, ER and NEP at low precipitation (<=400 mm) or low wetness (De Martonne WI <= 30), but not significantly at >400 mm or WI > 30. AGB fell by 27.9% (light), 34.6% (moderate) and 66.2% (heavy grazing). In an Inner Mongolia steppe experiment, light grazing raised NEP by 85.8% in the wettest year but not in drier years.
unit: % AGB change, light grazing vs ungrazed (all conditions)
locator: p.9 sec 3.2 (Fig. 5B, Fig. 6, Fig. S10A); p.9 sec 3.1 field results
note: Grazing vs exclusion, not rotational vs continuous: indirect for G1.2. Stress as defined by the source: Mean annual precipitation <=400 vs >400 mm; De Martonne wetness index <=30 vs >30; wet vs dry years in the field experiment. Not peer reviewed (eLife reviewers flag incomplete meta-analysis reporting). Compares grazing intensity vs exclusion, not rotational vs continuous, so it bears only on the stocking-rate part of G1.2. Mostly China and temperate data. Grazing harm is larger in dry conditions, which supports stocking at or below capacity.

finding: Under high water stress (<40% of crop water requirement), biochar raised yield by 33.0%, versus roughly 9% under moderate stress (40-70%) and roughly 8% with no stress (>70%), read from Fig. 4. The authors state the high-stress effect was 182% and 309% greater than under moderate and no stress. Biochar raised WUE by 17.9/22.6/22.2% (high/moderate/none).
unit: % yield increase vs no biochar, high water stress
locator: p.6 sec 3.3; p.7 Fig. 4 (moderate and no-stress yield values read from figure); p.4 sec 3.1
note: Stress as defined by the source: Water supply as % of crop requirement: high stress <40%, moderate 40-70%, none >70% (imposed irrigation regimes). Mostly greenhouse pot trials (16/25), mostly China; small sample, and missing SEs were set to 1% of the mean. The moderate and no-stress values are approximate (from the figure). Gives a clear direction (bigger effect under drought) but magnitudes are not field-transferable.

finding: Agroforestry reduced 'climate-related yield loss' in coffee: OR 0.67 (0.56-0.80), I2 = 0% (abstract and Table 1). The section 3.2 text gives OR 0.69 (0.58-0.82) from 28 studies. Pest and disease incidence OR 0.79 and quality degradation OR 0.74. No drought vs heat split; no significant moderators (region, zone).
unit: odds ratio of climate-related yield loss (AF vs non-AF)
locator: Abstract; sec 3.2, Table 1; sec 3.3 (meta-regression); via WebFetch of publisher HTML
note: Hazard keyed to drought for the register; the paper pools drought, heat and other climate losses. Stress as defined by the source: 'observed or projected effects of climate variability' (stressor not defined; drought, heat and rainfall mixed). LOW QUALITY: internal inconsistencies (OR 0.67 vs 0.69; n 23 vs 28), implausible I2 = 0%, and mixes model and review studies. Its '2-4 C canopy cooling' claim is cited (Meylan 2017; Lin 2008), not derived. Use only as a weak signal.

finding: Across 36 Mediterranean field trials, trees reduced crop yield on average (light competition). Among management factors including 'imposed warming and drought', only fertilisation significantly improved the agroforestry response; the authors only suggest 'facilitation could be expected under extreme climate events'.
note: Hazard keyed to drought; the moderator pooled imposed warming and drought. Stress as defined by the source: Imposed warming and drought treatments as a categorical moderator (not significant). Outside SSA. Imposed drought/warming did not change the tree effect significantly; few trials. Full text is CC BY (Springer blocked automated fetch).

finding: Kongwa (Manyusi), Tanzania rainout-shelter trial (2019): under fertilised conditions drought significantly reduced maize grain yield in sole maize and maize-pigeonpea but not in maize-gliricidia or maize-gliricidia-pigeonpea; maize drought resistance (yield loss to drought) was higher in maize-gliricidia-pigeonpea than in sole maize and maize-pigeonpea. Without fertiliser no system showed a significant drought effect and resistance did not differ among systems. Intercrops were 'not more prone to yield loss with drought'.
locator: Results, Crop Yields; Fig. 3A-B; per-treatment losses only in Fig. 3B and Supplementary Table 2
note: Stress as defined by the source: Above-canopy rainout shelters intercepting 50 % of incoming rain from maize tasselling through maize and pigeonpea harvest (anthesis + grain fill); season slightly above the 425 mm 30-yr mean. Single season, 3 reps, split-split plot. Numeric yield losses by system are only in figures/supplement (not extracted); data on Harvard Dataverse doi 10.7910/DVN/G4QLNP behind a guestbook form (not filled). Shelters cut PAR 15.8 %. Gliricidia trial previously established by ICRAF; not on A1 list.

finding: Same Kongwa trial: pigeonpea grain yield (0.39-1.09 t/ha) was not affected by imposed drought in any system; maize-pigeonpea was the only intercrop with mean LER > 1 across water and fertiliser levels, 'particularly under drought'; fertilised maize in maize-pigeonpea lost yield to drought as in sole maize (no buffering of the maize component). Drought cut 0-20 cm soil moisture by 12.5 % on average and intercropping did not raise soil moisture.
locator: Abstract; Results (Crop Yields, Soil moisture); Fig. 2A, Fig. 3C-D, Fig. 4D
note: Stress as defined by the source: 50 % rain interception from maize tasselling to harvest. Mapping uncertain: pigeonpea here is an additive grain-legume intercrop, not a cover crop/green manure as in C2.1 definition. Value is the shelter effect on soil moisture, not a practice contrast.

finding: Chitedze RS, Malawi, 2016-17 (La Nina), 19-day pre-anthesis rainout-shelter drought: predicted grain yield losses vs open plots were 22.6 % conventional (CP, 3272 to 2532 kg/ha), 22.3 % no-till+mulch (NT), 20.5 % NT+cowpea rotation (CArot) and 23.1 % NT+cowpea intercrop (CAint); all CA treatments still out-yielded CP under the 19-day drought (posthoc). Drought x treatment interactions were not significant.
unit: percent maize yield loss, 19-day shelter drought (conventional 22.6; CA systems 20.5-23.1)
note: Losses computed by A2 from the regression terms in Table 2 (intercept + treatment + drought + interaction); the authors do not report them as percentages: Pending expert review. The lead author is on the CC4A team, so the source is not independent of the team. Chitedze CA trial (CIMMYT) is not in A1's trial list: candidate trial_id for A1. Stress as defined by the source: Large in-situ polythene rainout shelters (90 m2) erected 19 days before/around anthesis (La Nina 2016-17); shelters also raised Tmax by 2.7 C. Losses computed by this compiler from Table 2 regression coefficients (intercept + treatment + drought + interaction), not reported by the authors as %. CA advantage is absolute (higher yield level) rather than proportional. Trial established 2007; not on A1 list. Author overlap with requesting team (lead author).

finding: Same trial, 27-day rainout-shelter drought (2016-17): drought cut CP grain yield by 1788 kg/ha (p=0.003); predicted proportional losses were 54.6 % CP, 60.1 % NT, 62.5 % CArot and 47.1 % CAint, with significant negative extra losses for NT (-1599 kg/ha) and CArot (-3343 kg/ha); no significant differences between treatments or vs control under the 27-day drought - 'the resistance benefit of CA was no-longer significant'. Surface soil moisture fell 54.5 % (0-5 cm) and 18.7 % at 100 cm.
unit: percent maize yield loss, 27-day shelter drought (conventional 54.6; CA systems 47.1-62.5)
note: Losses computed by A2 from the regression terms in Table 2 (intercept + treatment + drought + interaction); the authors do not report them as percentages: Pending expert review. The lead author is on the CC4A team, so the source is not independent of the team. Chitedze CA trial (CIMMYT) is not in A1's trial list: candidate trial_id for A1. Stress as defined by the source: Rainout shelters for 27 days around anthesis, 2016-17. Proportional losses computed by compiler from Table 2. Under severe drought CA (except intercrop) lost a larger share of its higher open-plot yield. n=4 per treatment.

finding: Natural drought, 2015-16 El Nino (season rainfall 463 mm, 55.9 % of the 2005-2015 average): open-plot grain yield was 1555 kg/ha under conventional practice vs 4627 (NT), 4850 (CArot) and 5671 kg/ha (CAint); an 18-day shelter drought on top had no significant effect. Authors: CA systems 'better resisted climate stress around anthesis'.
unit: kg/ha maize grain under conventional practice, El Nino 2015/16 (CA systems 4627-5671)
note: The lead author is on the CC4A team. Stress as defined by the source: 2015-16 strong El Nino, 463 mm season rainfall (55.9 % of 2005-15 mean); shelter treatment 18-19 days from 43-62 DAP. No paired normal season at the same time; the 3x CA advantage in El Nino reflects 8 years of prior CA management as well as stress buffering. Stress-season row only.

finding: Sub-humid Zimbabwe rainfall-manipulation trial (2022-23 near-normal; 2023-24 El Nino): 30 % rainfall reduction decreased maize yield by 22 % in 2022-23 but increased it by 20 % in 2023-24; residue mulch (6 t DM/ha) 'provided no buffering effect' and reduced maize biomass and N uptake by about one-third in the dry 2023-24 season.
unit: approx. percent change in maize biomass with mulch, El Nino season 2023-24
note: Stress as defined by the source: Rain-exclusion reducing rainfall 30 %; plus natural El Nino 2023-24 dry, uneven season. Mulch on (apparently) tilled soil, not full CA (no-till) - partial match to C2.2. Factorial with N; 2 seasons only. Licence per OpenAlex/Crossref.

finding: Pennsylvania (USA) organic trial 2013-15 with rain-exclusion shelters from early July: drought reduced maize kernel yield by 33 % (2014) and 17 % (2015); cover crops 'neither ameliorated nor exacerbated drought stress' and there was no cover crop x moisture interaction for yield; cereal rye reduced yield up to 43 % relative to legume-containing covers.
unit: percent maize yield loss to imposed drought, same across cover-crop treatments
note: Stress as defined by the source: Rain-exclusion shelters from early July (maize mid-season). Outside Africa; cover crops incorporated with full inversion tillage (authors suggest more benefit with long-term use and surface residues). Abstract read via search summary.

finding: Rainout shelters in a 36-year rotation x tillage trial (Ontario, Canada): diversifying maize-soybean rotations with small grains and cover crops mitigated maize leaf/canopy water stress and 'reduced yield losses to drought by 17.1 +/- 6.1 %'.
unit: percentage-point reduction in maize yield loss to drought (mean +/- SE)
note: Stress as defined by the source: In-field rainout shelters within long-term experiment (temperate). Treatment is rotation diversification including red clover/cover crops, not cover crops alone - partial match to C2.1. low/high = mean +/- 1 SE. Outside Africa.

finding: Same Canadian rainout-shelter study: 'no-till did not affect maize drought resistance' (no difference in yield loss to imposed drought between no-till and conventional tillage).
note: Stress as defined by the source: In-field rainout shelters within 36-yr rotation x tillage trial. Temperate, outside Africa; residue status of no-till not stated in abstract.

finding: Ghana (Acrisol), 2017-2018 field trial of rice-straw biochar (0, 15, 30 t/ha) x irrigation (100 %, 60 %, 0 %): B30 gave the highest total dry matter yield, intercepted PAR and RUE, significantly above B0 in both seasons; irrigation regime had no effect in 2017 but no irrigation significantly reduced TDMY, IPAR and RUE in the drier 2018 season.
note: Stress as defined by the source: Deficit (60 % of full) and no irrigation vs full irrigation to field capacity every 3-4 days (TDR-based). Abstract does not report biochar x irrigation interaction or grain yield; dry matter only. 30 t/ha is far above realistic rates.

finding: Two-season field experiment (Nigeria, inferred) with irrigation at 100, 80 and 60 % of the amount needed to restore field capacity x biochar (0, 20 t/ha) x fertiliser: biochar plus fertiliser significantly raised grain yield, biomass and water-use efficiencies at every irrigation level, but the biochar x irrigation interaction was not significant (no extra benefit specifically under deficit).
note: Stress as defined by the source: Deficit irrigation at 80 % and 60 % of full irrigation requirement. Abstract read via RePEc/search summaries only. Site not stated in abstract; authors are at a Nigerian university (location inferred, unverified). Irrigated dry-season design.

finding: Rainfall-reduction shelters in a 27-year tree-based intercropping system and paired monoculture (southern Ontario): soybean yield in the tree-crop zone was stable under reduced rainfall, whereas only the monoculture yield dropped significantly; share of N from fixation was ~91 % (agroforestry) vs ~63 % (monocrop), though total fixed N fell under reduced rain in both. Absolute yields were lower near trees.
note: Also cited by IPCC AR6 WG2 ch. 5 (Rural Scan unit ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4). Stress as defined by the source: Rainfall-reduction shelters throughout the growing season. Abstract read only via search-engine summary (HAL/Springer blocked); yield numbers not extracted. Temperate.

finding: Western North Region, Ghana, 12-yr-old cocoa, 33 months: 2/3 rainwater suppression cut dry bean yield to <50 % of full-rainwater plots; 40 % shade raised dry bean yield by 12-45 % at all suppression levels, but shade x water interactions were not significant for yield (effects 'mainly additive'): shade benefits cocoa but does not protect it from drought.
unit: % higher dry bean yield under 40 % shade vs full sun at each suppression level (additive; no interaction)
locator: p.9 Section 3.4; Fig. 6; Table A.4; Table 1
note: Also Rural Scan unit ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2. Stress as defined by the source: Plastic panels ~1 m high diverting 1/3 or 2/3 of throughfall (Apr 2018-Mar 2021; fully effective from May 2019); leaf water potential reached -1.5 MPa in full sun. Shade from 40 % shade nets at 6.5 m, not shade trees (no root competition). Per-level yields only in Fig. 6/Table A.4 (not extracted). Pods: suppression reduced pod weight ~10 % in sun vs ~8 % in shade.

finding: Same Ghana experiment: shade nets lowered sub-canopy temperature by 1.5-3.1 C on average (full-sun below-canopy temperatures reached 42 C in March-April), raised RH by 4-11 % and lowered VPD by 0.04-0.28 kPa; soil moisture was higher under shade, especially in deeper layers.
unit: C cooler sub-canopy air under 40 % shade
note: Stress as defined by the source: Ambient heat; Tmax below canopy up to 42 C in full sun. Mechanism (microclimate), not yield. Artificial shade, not trees. Page locator approximate.

finding: Forest-savannah transition, Ghana, 2015/16 extreme drought: all cocoa under Albizia ferruginea shade died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77 % mortality, while full-sun cocoa kept higher sap flux (170 vs 115 g cm-2 d-1) and recovered better (163 vs 37); soil water was higher in full sun, implicating competition for water.
unit: percent cocoa mortality under shade trees in 2015/16 (Antiaris 77, Albizia 100)
note: Also Rural Scan unit ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1. Stress as defined by the source: Natural 2015/16 El Nino extreme drought (not imposed). Already registered as S-ABDULAI2017 (applicability); this row adds hazard_mitigation numbers only (negative: shade worsened drought outcome). Full-sun mortality not given in abstract. Natural, not imposed stress.

finding: Northern Ghana, four consecutive wet and dry seasons: a ~20-day drainage at flowering (soil kept >60 % saturation) reduced yield by 13-26 % in the dry season but not in the wet season; it raised inner-canopy temperature at flowering by only 0.2-0.3 C and spikelet sterility by 3-5 %, but raised canopy temperature from solar noon to midnight by 0.7-0.9 C around sunset in the dry season.
unit: percent grain yield, drained at flowering vs flooded, hot dry season (0 in wet season)
note: Stress as defined by the source: Dry season (hot) vs wet season; heat via canopy temperature at flowering and evening. Opposite sign: water-saving drainage at flowering increased heat exposure and yield loss in the hot dry season. Single drainage at flowering, not repeated AWD cycles.

finding: Pot study in glasshouse chambers (Wuhan, China), 4 varieties: high daytime temperature at panicle initiation (peak 37 vs 32 C, 15 days) cut grain yield by on average ~36 % under continuous flooding (26.5 to 16.9 g/plant) vs ~29 % when AWD was applied at tillering (32.1 to 22.7 g/plant); losses under CF were 63/55/32/5 % vs 38/39/37/7 % under AWD by variety; AWD lowered panicle temperature by 0.6-1.8 C under heat.
unit: percent yield loss to imposed heat: continuous flooding 36, AWD at tillering 29 (variety means)
note: Averages computed by the A2 search from Table 1: Pending expert review. Stress as defined by the source: HDT 7:00-19:00 peaking 37 C (measured daily max 38.4 C) for 15 days from panicle development stage 2; control peak 32 C. POT STUDY (flag). AWD only at tillering; averages and AWD losses computed by compiler from Table 1. Outside Africa.

finding: Pot study, Malaysia: with half-rate NPK and a 20-day drought at flowering (40 % field capacity), adding 50 t/ha basalt raised yield per pot to 49.90 g/m2 vs 20.56 g/m2 without basalt (authors state '58.80 % increment'), comparable to full-rate NPK; differences across treatments were largely not significant (shared letters).
unit: g/m2 grain per pot under drought with basalt (20.56 without)
locator: Section 2.6 (drought induction); Section 3.2.8 and Fig. 16 (pp.9-10); Table 1
note: Stress as defined by the source: Soil moisture held at 40 % field capacity from 88 to 108 DAS (flowering), all treatments except full-NPK control. POT STUDY (flag); no well-watered basalt/no-basalt pair, so buffering vs nutrient effect cannot be separated; treatment labels inconsistent between table and text; % stated by authors does not match the yields (would be ~143 %). 50-200 t/ha rates. Conference paper.

finding: Eastern DR Congo (South-Kivu, Tanganyika), four sites, Nov 2022-Oct 2023: hybrid Urochloa cultivars yielded up to 18.25-18.69 t DM/ha/yr (Cobra) vs 11.69 t DM/ha/yr for the local check Rhodes grass; Mulato II performed best in the dry season and Cobra and Mulato II combined high biomass with 'strong resistance to drought'.
unit: t DM/ha/yr best Urochloa hybrid (Rhodes grass check 11.69)
note: Stress as defined by the source: Natural dry season vs rainy season (not imposed). Forage yield only (no livestock output); one year; seasonal split numbers not extracted (Wiley blocked). Best available improved-vs-local forage drought contrast found; no rainout-shelter forage trial with a local comparator found in SSA.

finding: Communal feedlots, Eastern Cape, South Africa, 60 cattle in 3 groups (control, artificial shade, water spraying): shade lowered rectal temperature 39.5 to 38.8 C, respiration 60.4 to 52.3 breaths/min, panting score 2.8 to 1.5, and raised ADG 0.88 to 0.94 kg/d (+6.8 %) with FCR 8.5 to 7.8; water cooling did slightly better (ADG +11.4 %).
unit: % higher ADG with shade vs no shade (computed from Table 2)
note: Stress as defined by the source: Summer heat with THI frequently > 72 and mid-day > 80 (THI by treatment not reported). Artificial shade structures in feedlots, not trees/silvopasture (mechanism proxy only). Internal inconsistencies: abstract ADG +18 %/FCR 12 % do not match tables; breed description inconsistent.

finding: Field rain-exclusion (-30 %) in a Spanish dehesa over three years: net primary productivity fell 13 % under reduced rainfall, and habitats under tree canopy and in open grassland 'responded similarly' (no buffering of NPP by trees); under-canopy pasture was less productive (351 vs 493 g/m2) but more digestible (44 vs 41 %).
unit: % NPP change under 30 % rainfall reduction (same under trees and in open)
note: Stress as defined by the source: Rain-exclusion shelters reducing rainfall 30 %, three consecutive years. Mediterranean, outside Africa; pasture not livestock output;

finding: Same dehesa experiment, open-top chambers (+2-3 C): warming raised NPP 33 % in both habitats but reduced biomass digestibility by 7.5 %, an effect that occurred only in open grassland and not under tree canopy, 'suggesting a buffering role of trees'.
unit: % change in pasture digestibility under +2-3 C warming in open grassland (no change under trees)
note: Stress as defined by the source: Open-top chambers raising temperature 2-3 C. Forage quality, not quantity or animal output; outside Africa.

finding: Meta-analysis of 2010–2019 literature: biochar cut bulk density by 9% on average; field capacity rose 51% and wilting point 47% in coarse-textured soils, 13% and 9% in medium soils, and FC was unchanged in fine soils. Plant-available water rose about 45% (coarse), 21% (medium) and 14% (fine): 'improvement in plant available water content decreased with soil fineness'.
unit: % change in plant-available water content (coarse to fine soils)
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: none: soil water-retention property, not measured in a stress season. Soil property, not yield. FC/WP figures read in the abstract; the PAW by-texture figures (45/21/14%) come from a library-catalogue copy of the abstract, so check them against the full text. Mixed lab, pot and field studies; application rates often far above realistic farm rates.

finding: Meta-analysis of 89 studies (391 paired comparisons): cover crops increased infiltration rate by 34.8% (95% CI 19.8 to 50.0%; 81 comparisons from 23 studies). No difference in the cover-crop effect by annual rainfall or aridity index.
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: none: infiltration measured in field trials, not tied to a stress season. Africa study count not reported in the text (North America 31, Asia 27 studies). Infiltration is a mechanism for capturing rain, not a measure of yield under drought.

finding: Same meta-analysis: no-till overall +5.7% infiltration (CI −13.3 to 24.7%, not significant); no-till with residue retained +41.5% (CI −3.4 to 86.6%; 11 experiments); no-till in 600–1000 mm rainfall +55.6% (CI 5.8 to 105.3%). No-till reduced infiltration in more arid sites (lower aridity index), not significantly.
unit: % change in infiltration rate, no-till with residue retention (95% CI)
locator: Results 'No-Till'; Fig 4; Fig 5; Table 2; Fig E in S1 File
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: none; contrast by aridity index and annual rainfall class. The sign may reverse in drier sites (not significant): relevant because CA drought buffering is claimed mainly for dry areas.

finding: Dryland meta-analysis (38 articles; 539 soil-water and 1006 yield observations, 1994–2021): cover crops vs fallow reduced soil water content at cash-crop sowing by 18%, soil mineral N by 25% and cash-crop yield by 7%. Yield changes were +15% (tropical), +4% (continental), −12% (dry) and −11% (temperate) climates; ~700 mm annual rainfall is the 'break-even' for yield benefit.
unit: percent soil water at cash-crop sowing, cover crop vs fallow (yield -12 % in dry climates)
note: Stress as defined by the source: dryland climates; split by Köppen class and annual precipitation (~700 mm threshold). OPPOSITE SIGN for drought: cover crops deplete stored soil water in dry climates. Comparator is fallow (sequential cover crop), not relay or intercropped cover typical of SSA; full text not opened (publisher bot check).

finding: On-station CA trials 2005–2007: direct-seeded CA plots infiltrated 49% and 45% more water than conventionally tilled plots in two seasons at Henderson (Zimbabwe), and 57% and 87% more at Monze (Zambia). Soil moisture was higher through the season in most CA treatments. At Monze in 2005/06 a period of moisture stress at tasselling 'affected CA treatments less'; neither season had a significant drought, so drought mitigation was not tested directly.
unit: percent more infiltration under CA (Henderson 45-49, Monze 57-87)
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: moisture stress at tasselling, Monze 2005/06 (no formal drought definition). Zambian component is TR-MONZE-2005; Henderson (Zimbabwe) CA trial not found in the trial list. Abstract read via repository record.

finding: Continuous soil-moisture sensors on a smallholder farm in semi-arid Kenya, plus a calibrated model over two years: maize residue mulch increased the number of days when root-zone relative soil moisture stayed above the maize water-stress limit by 24–46%. Model: mulch thicker than 1 cm could have kept soil moisture above the stress limit through a 19-day dry spell; thickening from 1 to 3 cm added 59% more unstressed days.
unit: percent more days with root-zone soil moisture above the maize stress limit (mulch vs bare)
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: relative soil moisture below maize water-stress limit s*; a 19-day dry spell in the record. Mulch vs bare soil only (no tillage contrast); one farm; part of the result is modelled.

finding: Mulched vs unmulched tropical luvisol and cambisol, 1970–72: early in the season soil temperature at 5 cm was up to 8 °C lower under mulch; mulch also raised soil moisture. Grain yield rose 46%, 52% and 22% in 1970, 1971 and 1972, attributed mainly to lower soil temperature.
unit: °C soil temperature at 5 cm (maximum difference, early growth)
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: supra-optimal seedbed temperature (no threshold given in abstract). Residue mulch, not full CA. IITA study; Nigeria location assumed from author affiliation, not stated in the abstract read via AGRIS/search excerpt. Predates TR-IBADAN-1976.

finding: Hydraulic redistribution was detected in 46% of psychrometer readings under karité (Vitellaria paradoxa) and 33% under néré (Parkia biglobosa) in the 2004 and 2005 dry seasons. A modified WaNuLCAS model put redistributed water at about 73.0 (karité) and 247.1 (néré) L per tree per day in 2005, about 60% and 53% of daily transpiration; the authors say the model probably overestimates these volumes.
unit: L water redistributed per tree per day (modelled)
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: dry season (no crop present). Original study behind the van Noordwijk 2021 Rural Scan unit. Dry-season mechanism; does not show crop benefit during an in-season drought. Abstract read via CIFOR-ICRAF record.

finding: Under néré and karité canopies in Burkina Faso, millet seedlings experienced only 1–9 h per week of supra-optimal temperatures (>40 °C), against 27 h per week in the open. PAR under canopies fell to 24% of incident, yet millet biomass did not differ from the open. Wind and soil evaporation were lower under trees, but water was not limiting (920 mm rain).
unit: fewer hours per week above 40 °C under canopy than in open
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: seedling temperature >40 °C (supra-optimal). Single wet season (920 mm), so the heat benefit was not tested in a drought year. Range computed from 27 h minus 1–9 h.

finding: Topsoil (0–15 cm) moisture was higher under Faidherbia albida canopies in central Malawi; the canopy-vs-open difference grew from about 4% at the start of the cropping season to about 50% at the end.
unit: % higher topsoil moisture under canopy than open (start to end of season)
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: end-of-season soil drying (no drought defined). Abstract seen only through a search-engine excerpt; verify. Faidherbia is leafless in the rainy season, so the shade effect is small; the moisture effect may come from soil organic matter and infiltration.

finding: TDR monitoring to 420 cm in the Sob Faidherbia albida parkland (Senegal), July–October 2020: 'The higher water content for both SSM and DSM was observed outside the FA canopy' (shallow 20–60 cm and deep 70–420 cm layers), and soil water content was positively correlated with distance from the tree regardless of slope position, refuting the authors' hypothesis.
unit: direction only: soil water content higher outside canopy
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: rainy season, no drought defined. OPPOSITE SIGN to Rhoades 1995 and Clermont-Dauphin 2023. Conference abstract, not peer reviewed; one season. Site matches TR-SOB-2018.

finding: ICRAF Machakos (Kenya), dispersed Grevillea robusta over maize, 1995/96 short rains: maximum maize meristem temperature was 6 °C lower than in unshaded sole maize, and the tree effect was similar to a 25% shade net; the open crop had a mean diurnal range of 20 °C. The cooling effect declined as trees grew taller and were pruned up. The review notes that meristem temperatures at Machakos 'persistently exceed the optimum only during periods of drought'.
unit: °C maximum maize meristem temperature vs unshaded sole maize
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Keyed to C3.2: Grevillea was planted and dispersed within the maize field (intercropping), not a retained parkland tree; Lott 2009 (Rural Scan row) is the same Machakos system. Stress as defined by the source: supra-optimal meristem temperature (no threshold value given). Review summarising Lott et al. 2000a,b (primary). Grevillea is a dispersed exotic tree, closer to C3.1 than to alley cropping. No DOI seen. OpenAlex lists licence CC BY-NC-SA; not shown on the PDF. ICRAF Machakos station, not KARI Katumani (check against TR-KATUMANI-ALLEY-1989).

finding: Same Machakos Grevillea–maize system: although trees cut PAR to understorey maize by about 30% (similar to a 25% shade net), the yield loss was much greater than under the 25% shade net in four seasons with highly variable rainfall, so 'competition for water was an important factor limiting crop production in all seasons'. In the dry 1995 long rains (302 mm) maize photosynthesis and transpiration under trees were much lower than under the 25% shade net. The review also cites Leucaena alley cropping where competition for water outweighed soil-fertility benefits (Govindarajan et al. 1996, India).
unit: direction only: below-ground water competition reduces understorey maize, strongest in dry season
note: Keyed to C3.2 as above; Machakos Grevillea-maize, not the Katumani Leucaena trial (TR-KATUMANI-ALLEY-1989). Stress as defined by the source: 1995 long rains, 302 mm (dry) vs 1994/95 short rains, 628 mm. OPPOSITE SIGN for drought (tree water competition), also relevant to C3.2 alley cropping. Review of Lott et al. 2000b and others; yield numbers not given in the review text.

finding: Chiapas (Mexico) coffee sites at high (60–80%), medium (35–65%) and low (10–30%) shade: seasonal means differed little, but fluctuations in temperature, humidity and solar radiation increased significantly as shade cover decreased, and the low-shade site had significantly larger swings in soil moisture gain and loss. Shade cover was 'directly related to the mitigation of variability'.
unit: direction only: microclimate and soil-moisture variability fall with shade
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: microclimate extremes (no threshold). Outside Africa. Abstract read through search excerpts (publisher blocked); peak-hour (10:00–14:00) cooling reported only in a university press release, not used here.

finding: Eight common shade-tree species in cocoa farms in Ahafo, Ghana: species varied strongly in sub-canopy microclimate. Mangifera indica and Milicia excelsa let through the least light and gave the strongest buffering, reducing vapour pressure deficit and daily swings in temperature and relative humidity. Cocoa grew better further from the shade-tree stem.
unit: direction only: shade species reduce VPD and temperature range
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: none defined. Numbers are in the full text, not opened (publisher bot check). Distance effect shows a competition trade-off.

finding: Pot experiment (Wuhan, China, 2019): AWD at tillering (re-irrigate at −20 kPa, 7 cycles) vs continuous flooding (2–3 cm), then high daytime temperature (peak 37 °C, mean daily max 38.4 °C) for 15 days at panicle initiation. Under heat, AWD lowered panicle temperature by 1.8 °C (LYPJ), 1.1 °C (IR64), 0.7 °C (HHZ) and 0.6 °C (SY63), measured by infrared thermography on day 10.
unit: °C panicle temperature, AWD minus continuous flooding, under heat
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Pot study. Yield under heat from the same experiment is in the imposed-stress row for Gao 2025. Stress as defined by the source: greenhouse high daytime temperature, peak 37 °C 11:00–15:00 for 15 d at panicle initiation (control peak 32 °C). Pot study in glasshouses. AWD applied only before the heat; water status during the heat is not stated. AWD also lowered panicle temperature by 0.5–1.1 °C without heat. The mechanism is attributed to roots and cytokinins, not field-water cooling.

finding: Field trial (Hunan, China, 2017–18), treatments from booting to maturity: compared with 8–10 cm standing water, mild soil drying (−20 to −30 kPa) shrank the panicle–air, leaf–air and canopy–air temperature differences by 1.16, 0.65 and 0.71 °C (severe drying −40 to −50 kPa: 1.68, 1.16, 1.05 °C), i.e. less transpirational cooling, during grain filling. Yield fell 9.5–14.4% under mild and 28.7–35.1% under severe drying, and rose 8.8–12.3% under shallow (1–3 cm) water.
unit: °C loss of organ-below-air cooling under soil drying vs deep flooding
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: soil water potential −20 to −30 kPa (mild) and −40 to −50 kPa (severe) from booting to maturity; no heat event defined. OPPOSITE direction to Gao 2025 for late-season drying: continuous deficit from booting to maturity, harsher than safe AWD (−15 kPa with reflooding). Supports the view that drained fields lose canopy cooling in the heat-sensitive window. Text reports temperature differences, not absolute values.

finding: First evidence synthesis of ERW effects on the soil 'sponge function' (17 studies, 261 treatment–control observations, descriptive medians): field capacity +9.4% (n=23 from 5 studies), plant-available water +10.1% (n=15 from 3), dynamic soil moisture +4.4% (n=21 from 4), Ksat −27.5% (2 studies), porosity −6.3%, infiltration 0.0%. 'ERW does not uniformly enhance the soil sponge function'. Includes two Ghana studies (Akortey et al. 2026 greenhouse; Obour et al. 2024 pot/field).
unit: median % change (PAW; range to soil moisture)
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: none: soil properties. Preprint, not peer reviewed. Mixed rock types (basalt, glacial rock flour, gneiss, metabasalt) and many pot/lab studies; a long-term basalt field trial (Pihlap et al. 2025) showed small negative FC and PAW responses.

finding: Meta-analysis of 145 experiments on stressed plants given silicon (Si): across plant families and abiotic stresses (drought among them), Si increased dry weight, net assimilation rate and chlorophyll biosynthesis and consistently reduced oxidative damage; responses depended on plant family (Si accumulator type) and stress type.
unit: direction only: Si increases biomass and assimilation under abiotic stress
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Silicon salts, not basalt: a mechanism link to C4.1 only. Stress as defined by the source: experimentally imposed abiotic stresses (drought, salinity, metals etc.). Mechanism link only: soluble Si supply, mostly pot/hydroponic. Whether basalt dust supplies enough plant-available Si in the field is not shown. Drought-only effect sizes are not in the abstract.

finding: Review plus meta-analysis of 15 shade vs no-shade comparisons (9 articles) in summer feedlots: shade raised ADG by 0.07 ± 0.021 kg/d (1.48 vs 1.41 kg/d), gain efficiency by 3.4% and hot carcass weight by 5.8 kg, with no change in DMI (8.58 vs 8.74 kg/d). The review finds shaded cattle have lower respiration rate, panting score and body temperature under heat load, with smaller benefit in Bos indicus.
unit: kg/d extra average daily gain with shade
note: Artificial feedlot shade, not trees: a proxy for the shade part of G2.1. Stress as defined by the source: summer months, hot weather (studies chosen for greatest heat load; THI not pooled). Artificial feedlot shade, mostly dark-hided Bos taurus in the USA; authors flag bias toward positive results. Pasture and tree-shade evidence is thinner. Brahman cattle showed minimal shade effect.

finding: Brazilian Cerrado, 48 lactating cows over two years in full sun vs Eucalyptus silvopasture: shaded cows had lower rectal and surface temperatures, respiration rates and panting scores, 'with significant differences amplified under heat stress conditions (THI > 74)'. Gyr (Bos indicus) thermoregulated better than Girolando.
unit: direction only: lower body temperature and respiration rate under tree shade
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: THI > 74. Physiology only; milk yield not in abstract. Full text not opened (publisher bot check).

finding: Systematic review (1,448 records screened, 19 included) of silvopastoral systems vs treeless pasture for dairy cows: SPS gave a more comfortable thermal environment linked to more feeding behaviour; cows in SPS showed fewer drinking events and lower surface temperature and respiratory rate. Nine behavioural and physiological variables (e.g. rumination, internal temperature) were unclear, and milk production was measured in only two studies.
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: not pooled; thermal comfort indices. No pooled effect sizes. Mostly Latin American studies. Abstract read via the Nottingham veterinary systematic-review database.

finding: Greenhouse soil-column study, 21 days of progressive drying: drought cut shoot dry mass of both Napier grass and Brachiaria hybrid Mulato II by about 35%. Mulato II closed stomata early at relatively wet soil and left water in the soil ('water-saving'), while Napier transpired most available water ('water-spending'). Root dry mass fell 50% in Mulato II vs 20% in Napier.
unit: % shoot dry mass under drought vs well watered (both grasses)
note: Pot study; improved Brachiaria vs Napier (the usual improved comparator in East Africa), not vs the current diet. Stress as defined by the source: progressive soil drying for 21 days from field capacity. Pot study (CIAT, Colombia). finding: Five seasons across South Africa's central grassland and Kalahari savanna: in the savanna, 'irrespective of rainfall', rotational grazing gave higher phytomass and phytomass–cover ratios than continuous grazing. In the grassland the difference appeared only in the phytomass–cover ratio and only in two years with above-average antecedent rainfall. Rangeland condition (increaser/decreaser species) did not differ with management in either biome.
unit: direction only: higher standing phytomass under rotational grazing (savanna)
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: annual rainfall and antecedent rainfall as covariates (no drought threshold). Comparison of farms under different management (observational), not a controlled trial.

finding: Severe 1982/83 drought in Eastern Cape semi-arid grassveld caused extensive grass mortality. Veld grazed immediately after the drought recovered much more slowly than veld that was rested, and the difference was still visible three years later. Increaser I grasses survived drought best, Decreasers next and Increaser II worst; recovery ran in the opposite order.
unit: direction only: post-drought rest speeds sward recovery
note: Mechanism evidence: a soil, microclimate or physiology effect, not yield under stress. Stress as defined by the source: severe drought, 1982/83 growing season. Supports the 'rest after drought' element of planned grazing, not rotation per se. Abstract seen via the Rangelands Gateway record and search excerpt; numbers not in the abstract.
